item.title: Gru's Plan: Naive Decision-Maker
item.author: gerrit.stahn93.gs4@gmail.com (Imprint)
item.description: Context: I use this meme in an exercise on time-inconsistent decision-making in behavioral economics. It clearly illustrates how individuals who heavily discount their future utility and who fail to predict their own later decisions are potentially worse off than sophisticated decision-makers, who realistically anticipate their future (lack of) self-control.

item.title: Back In My Day Meme: No Probability Weighting
item.author: gerrit.stahn93.gs4@gmail.com (Imprint)
item.description: Context: I use this meme in an undergraduate exercise on probability weighting as a segue into Prospect Theory. I find it particularly fitting because it also symbolizes how some classical economists react to the insights contributed by behavioral economics.

item.title: Tom Meme: Not Cooperating in a Sequential Game.
item.author: gerrit.stahn93.gs4@gmail.com (Imprint)
item.description: Context: I use this meme for an exercise in a bachelor-level course on sequential games to illustrate how this type of game can lead to pareto-inferior outcomes.

item.title: Bernie Meme: Is playing Powerball really worth it?
item.author: gerrit.stahn93.gs4@gmail.com (Imprint)
item.description: Context: I use this meme as an engaging opener for a bachelor-level microeconomics exercise on decision-making under uncertainty and risk. In that session, I explain the fundamentals of expected utility theory. Among other things, the students have to calculate the fair price of a German lottery ticket (6aus49). Since the German Lotto is comparable to Powerball, I’ve adjusted the meme slightly for my U.S. audience. 😉
